message.content:
In C, a **file** is simply a named sequence of bytes stored somewhere outside your program’s memory (on disk, flash, network, etc.).  
C gives you two families of APIs to work with files:

| API | Where it comes from | Typical use‑case |
|-----|--------------------|------------------|
| `FILE *` + `<stdio.h>` | Standard C library | Portable, buffered I/O (text & binary). |
| `int` + `<fcntl.h>` / `<unistd.h>` | POSIX (Unix/Linux) | Low‑level, unbuffered I/O; useful when you need fine control over flags, non‑blocking, async, etc. |

Below is a quick tour of the high‑level, portable interface (`<stdio.h>`), followed by a short look at the low‑level one.

---

## 1. High‑Level (Buffered) I/O – `FILE *`

### Opening a file

```c
#include <stdio.h>

FILE *fp = fopen("example.txt", "r");   // open for reading
if (!fp) {
    perror("fopen failed");
    return 1;
}
```

| Mode string | Meaning |
|-------------|---------|
| `"r"`       | Read only, text mode, fail if file doesn’t exist |
| `"w"`       | Write only, truncate or create, text mode |
| `"a"`       | Append only, create if missing, text mode |
| `"r+"`      | Read/write, fail if missing |
| `"w+"`      | Read/write, truncate or create |
| `"a+"`      | Read/append, create if missing |
| Add `"b"`   | Binary mode (no translation of newline/EOF) |
| Add `"x"`   | Create exclusive (fail if exists) |

### Reading a file

#### Text mode – line by line

```c
char buffer[256];
while (fgets(buffer, sizeof buffer, fp)) {
    printf("%s", buffer);          // already contains '\n'
}
```

#### Binary mode – block by block

```c
unsigned char buf[1024];
size_t nread;
while ((nread = fread(buf, 1, sizeof buf, fp)) > 0) {
    /* process nread bytes */
}
```

### Writing a file

```c
fprintf(fp, "Hello %s!\n", name);   // formatted output
fwrite(data, 1, len, fp);           // raw bytes
```

### Seeking & telling

```c
fseek(fp, 0, SEEK_SET);            // go to beginning
long pos = ftell(fp);               // current position
rewind(fp);                         // same as fseek(fp,0,SEEK_SET)
```

### Closing a file

```c
if (fclose(fp) != 0) {
    perror("fclose failed");
}
```

### Common pitfalls

| Problem | Fix |
|---------|-----|
| Forgetting to check `ferror()` after a loop | Call `feof()` and `ferror()` to distinguish EOF vs error |
| Mixing binary/text mode on Windows | Always add `"b"` for binary files |
| Using `fflush()` on input streams | Undefined behavior – don’t flush reads |

---

## 2. Low‑Level (Unbuffered) I/O – File Descriptors

If you need more control (e.g., non‑blocking sockets, `select`, `poll`, `mmap`), use POSIX calls:

```c
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <unistd.h>

int fd = open("example.bin", O_RDONLY);
if (fd == -1) { perror("open"); exit(1); }

ssize_t n;
char buf[512];
while ((n = read(fd, buf, sizeof buf)) > 0) {
    /* process n bytes */
}

close(fd);
```

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `O_RDONLY` | Read only |
| `O_WRONLY` | Write only |
| `O_RDWR`   | Read/write |
| `O_CREAT`  | Create if missing |
| `O_EXCL`   | Fail if exists (with `O_CREAT`) |
| `O_APPEND` | Append writes |
| `O_TRUNC`  | Truncate existing file |
| `O_NONBLOCK` | Non‑blocking I/O |

These functions operate on integer file descriptors (`int`). They’re unbuffered, so you’ll see the exact number of bytes requested unless an error occurs.

---

## 3. Summary

| Feature | Buffered (`FILE *`) | Unbuffered (`int`) |
|---------|---------------------|--------------------|
| Portability | ANSI C, works everywhere | POSIX, not on plain Windows |
| Buffering | Automatic, good for text | None, manual buffering needed |
| Modes | `"r/w/a/r+/w+/a+/*b*/x"` | Flags (`O_*`) |
| Error handling | `ferror()`, `perror()` | `errno`, `perror()` |
| Typical use | Text files, simple programs | Sockets, pipes, performance tuning |

Pick the one that matches your needs. For most everyday tasks (reading config files, writing logs, etc.) the `FILE *` interface is easier and safer. If you hit performance bottlenecks or need fine‑grained control, switch to the descriptor API.

Happy coding!
